old: Sensor-Aware Self-Supervised Transfer Learning for Label-Efficient Multigas Electronic Nose Calibration
new: Self-Supervised Transfer Learning for Label-Efficient Multigas Electronic Nose Calibration

old: Abstract— Precisely labeled gas mixtures require concentration control or reference quantification, whereas mixtures without carefully controlled ppm can provide inexpensive unlabeled sensor responses. This motivates self-supervised pretraining on a large unquantified mixture pool followed by calibration with a small precisely labeled set. The authors evaluate the label-efficiency premise using existing datasets with concentration labels withheld during pretraining. A shared temporal encoder, sensor-identity embeddings, cross-sensor attention, and structured masked reconstruction are evaluated with a predefined fine-tuned transfer policy and 10 seeds. Primary evaluation uses six held-partition NH3/H2 folds and three rolling chronological CO/ethylene folds. Relative MAE reductions against scratch are NH3 13.9%, H2 21.5%, CO 27.5%, Ethylene 25.7%. Paired seed-and-fold bootstrap intervals exclude zero for these four comparisons, conditional on the observed exposures. Fixed-split experiments compare all adaptation policies, calibration designs, classical regression, a compact PatchTST-style SSL control, architectural ablations, and window placement. The proposed architecture is not uniformly superior to generic SSL or classical models. Long-term drift evaluation includes constant controls, normalized errors, small budgets, and target-loss sensitivity; regression is conditional on known gas identity. These results support label-efficient same-system recalibration. Prospective pretraining on cheaply acquired, unquantified mixtures and its cost savings remain to be evaluated.
new: Abstract— Self-supervised transfer reduces mean absolute concentration error relative to training from scratch by 13.9% for NH3, 21.5% for H2, 27.5% for CO, and 25.7% for ethylene in our primary multigas electronic-nose evaluation. We pretrain a shared temporal encoder using masked sensor-response reconstruction, then fine-tune it with a limited set of labeled concentration pairs. The evaluation uses ten seeds, six held-out identifier partitions for NH3/H2, and three rolling chronological folds for CO/ethylene; the NH3/H2 results use a predefined early-response window. In secondary fixed-split experiments, fine-tuning with 10 labeled pairs gives approximately the NH3 and ethylene errors of scratch training with 20 pairs, a lower mean CO error, and a higher H2 error. These pair counts include validation labels. Sensor-identity and cross-sensor-attention ablations show target-dependent effects, with NH3 the weakest transfer case. In a known-gas-identity drift benchmark, transfer improves concentration regression in partitions 8 and 9 but not clearly in partition 10. The proposed model is not the best full-budget baseline on any of the four raw-response targets. The findings support target-dependent label efficiency for same-system calibration; the NH3/H2 identifier partitions do not establish between-day generalization.

old: The authors' contribution is a controlled evaluation of masked sensor-aware learning for quantitative same-system recalibration, with limited labels, held-out partitions, chronological tests and direct competing controls.
new: Our contribution is a controlled evaluation of masked self-supervised transfer for quantitative same-system recalibration, with limited labels, held-out identifier partitions, chronological tests and direct competing controls.

old: Three temporal spans are sampled per example to encourage inference of missing dynamics.
new: Here b indexes examples in a minibatch, t the temporal position, s the physical sensor, and k one of three spans sampled independently for each example. Given span width w_k, its start a_k is sampled uniformly from the integers 0 through T − w_k; the example index on a_k and w_k is suppressed. B_bks denotes sensor participation in span k. M is one for observed entries and zero for hidden entries.

old: The NH3/H2 dataset [29] contains 162,404 observations from 20 Nano MEMS sensor channels, grouped into 378 recorded sequences, with concentrations of 0–500 ppm for each gas. The authors form six partitions of 63 sequences using consecutive Combination identifiers; these partitions do not establish separate acquisition days or physically independent measurements.
new: The NH3/H2 dataset [29] contains 162,404 observations from 20 Nano MEMS sensor channels, grouped into 378 recorded sequences, with concentrations of 0–500 ppm for each gas. Acquisition took place over six days. The six partitions of 63 sequences were constructed from consecutive Combination identifiers and were not designed as day splits. Day-by-day mixture details were not logged, so a reliable exposure-to-day mapping and leave-one-day-out evaluation cannot be reconstructed. Training and test partitions may share acquisition days; these folds do not establish between-day generalization.

old: Dataset-specific hardware and environmental settings remain unverified; the related VOC-array study [28] does not establish the NH3/H2 acquisition configuration. Digital audits found no identical stored signal fingerprints or identifier overlap across 11 split definitions, but do not prove physical acquisition independence. The concentration range does not validate low-concentration ambient monitoring. Supplementary ?NH3/H2 dataset and acquisition details? provides the metadata limitations and audit scope.
new: The NH3/H2 array uses 20 MEMS SnO2 channels with Pt/Ag modification, as described in Supplementary “NH3/H2 dataset and acquisition details.” Temperature and relative humidity were neither controlled nor measured during acquisition, so their variation and contribution to response differences cannot be quantified retrospectively. Digital audits found no identical stored signal fingerprints or identifier overlap across 11 split definitions; they do not establish session independence. The 0–500 ppm range does not validate low-concentration ambient monitoring.

old: NH3/H2 sensitivity tests compare early, middle, late, and full-exposure 64-sample inputs, refitting scalers on the corresponding pretraining windows. Early windows remain predefined. Exact sample-position definitions are supplied in the supplement; without a verified sampling frequency, positions cannot be interpreted as durations.
new: Each NH3/H2 sequence starts at gas delivery and contains 180 s of exposure followed by 700 s of recovery. The configured sampling interval is 2.0 s. The predefined 64-sample early window covers about 128 s nominally (approximately 131 s from aggregate sample counts), or roughly 71–73% of exposure. Middle, late and full-cycle sensitivity inputs also have 64 samples, with scalers refitted on their pretraining windows. Full-cycle resampling includes recovery, rather than only the 180-s gas exposure. Exact index definitions and the approximate timing calculation are supplied in the supplement.

old: Table I compares fine-tuning with scratch under matched adaptation groups and holdouts. All four paired intervals exclude zero, with NH3 closest to zero. Inference is conditional on observed exposures, not new arrays or acquisition campaigns.
new: Table I compares fine-tuning with scratch under matched adaptation groups and holdouts. The four unadjusted paired 95% intervals exclude zero. In a four-comparison Bonferroni sensitivity analysis, the NH3 interval includes zero; the other three remain positive (Supplementary Table S9). NH3 is therefore the weakest primary case. CO/ethylene intervals are indicative because they resample only three chronological folds. Inference is conditional on observed exposures, not independent acquisition campaigns.

old: Random and farthest-point designs are crossed with both training policies at every budget. At five pairs, random minus farthest-point fine-tuned MAE is NH3: 3.74 ppm (95% interval -17.95 to 28.62); H2: 14.62 ppm (95% interval -5.72 to 35.31); CO: 31.61 ppm (95% interval 13.34 to 51.92); Ethylene: 0.855 ppm (95% interval -0.595 to 2.151). The design effect is therefore target-dependent. It uses known concentration coordinates and must not be interpreted as active acquisition of unknown labels. All-budget paired design and transfer contrasts are in Supplementary Table S3.
new: Calibration-design effects depend on both target and budget (Supplementary Table S3). At five pairs, farthest-point design reduces fine-tuned CO MAE relative to random by 31.61 ppm (unadjusted 95% interval 13.34–51.92). At 40 pairs, random design instead has lower MAE: random minus farthest-point differences are −4.46 ppm for NH3 and −8.32 ppm for H2 under scratch training, and −3.37 and −4.89 ppm under fine-tuning; all four exploratory intervals exclude zero. These are known-coordinate calibration designs, not active acquisition of unknown labels. Full-budget designs coincide when all candidate pairs are used.

old: The sensor-aware model is not uniformly strongest. PLSR CO MAE is 25.57 ± 8.48 ppm versus 47.45 ± 7.38 ppm for fine-tuning; Extra Trees ethylene MAE is 1.398 ± 0.197 ppm versus 1.627 ± 0.275 ppm. These are observed means under the declared fixed split, not a claim of universal statistical superiority. PLSR/SVR validation grids and all budget results are documented in the supplement.
new: The proposed model has the lowest mean MAE on none of the four targets at full budget (Table IV). Generic SSL leads on NH3 (16.13 versus 17.36 ppm), SVR on H2 (31.37 versus 31.60 ppm), Extra Trees on ethylene (1.398 versus 1.627 ppm), and PLSR on CO (25.57 versus 47.45 ppm). Proposed CO MAE is 1.86 times PLSR MAE despite improvement over scratch. A lower-complexity latent linear model may better suit the small calibration set and this response representation; this is a possible explanation, not an identified mechanism. Close mean rankings are not equivalence tests, and overlapping SDs do not establish statistical ties. Tuning grids and all-budget results are supplied in the supplement.

old: Window placement changes absolute error and transfer effects (Table VI): late windows are worse for both gases, and middle-window H2 does not improve. Full-exposure resampling is a control, not a test-selected optimum; early windows remain predefined.
new: Window placement materially changes both absolute error and transfer effects (Table VI). Fixed-split early-window H2 improves from 41.20 to 31.60 ppm (23.3%); middle-window transfer reverses the benefit (33.99 to 35.60 ppm, −4.7%); full-cycle resampling yields 38.36 to 35.75 ppm (6.8%). The 21.5% headline instead comes from primary multi-fold evaluation using the same predefined early-window definition. It should not be generalized to other window placements. Middle/late windows sample the recovery part of the recorded cycle; full-cycle resampling spans exposure and recovery. No window is selected using test performance.

old: Sensor-aware masked pretraining supports label-efficient same-system recalibration. Under predefined fine-tuning, primary multi-fold MAE reductions versus scratch are 13.9% for NH3, 21.5% for H2, 27.5% for CO and 25.7% for ethylene.
new: Masked self-supervised pretraining reduces mean error against scratch in this same-system calibration evaluation. Under predefined fine-tuning, primary reductions are 13.9% for NH3, 21.5% for H2, 27.5% for CO and 25.7% for ethylene; NH3/H2 uses the early-response window. Fixed-split pair-count comparisons show approximately comparable NH3/ethylene errors and lower mean CO error with 10 transfer pairs versus 20 scratch pairs, but not an H2 match at those budgets.

old: These gains do not establish architectural superiority: generic SSL and classical regressors outperform the proposed model on some targets. Ablation, window, calibration-design and budget effects are target-dependent. Remaining absolute and tail errors, especially for CO, limit practical calibration adequacy.
new: The proposed model is not the best full-budget baseline on any of the four targets; CO MAE is 1.86 times that of PLSR. Sensor identity and attention are not uniformly beneficial, particularly for NH3. NH3 also has negligible five-pair improvement and is the weakest multiplicity-adjusted primary case. Window and calibration-design effects vary with target and budget. Remaining absolute and tail errors limit quantitative usefulness.

old: Ten seeds quantify training/design variability, not independent acquisitions. Intervals condition on observed exposures; NH3 is close to zero, chronological folds are few and training folds overlap. Fixed-split estimates are seed-sensitive. Physical exposure independence and cross-device generalization require further evidence; sensor identities depend on channel correspondence.
new: Ten seeds quantify training/design variability, not independent acquisitions. NH3’s four-comparison adjusted interval includes zero; CO/ethylene intervals remain indicative with only three folds. NH3/H2 acquisition spanned six days, but missing day-by-day mixture logs prevent reliable day-held-out evaluation. Temperature and humidity were neither controlled nor measured. Consequently these identifier folds cannot establish between-day or environmental robustness. Cross-device transfer remains unevaluated.

old: Label withholding tests the learning premise retrospectively, not acquisition-cost savings. Known-coordinate calibration design excludes candidate-pool quantification costs. Prospective work should combine inexpensive unquantified mixtures, limited precise adaptation labels and independent quantified tests with cost accounting and acquisition metadata. Temporal adaptation and shift-aware uncertainty are further priorities.
new: Label withholding tests the learning premise retrospectively, not acquisition-cost savings. Known-coordinate calibration design excludes candidate-pool quantification costs. Future experiments will measure and record environmental conditions; exposure-linked day/session logs are needed for independent-day evaluation. Prospective unquantified-mixture pretraining, acquisition-cost accounting, and shift-aware uncertainty remain future work.

Both denominators in (14) are guarded against empty sets. In the present raw-response mask, at most 48 of 64 positions are covered by three spans and at most three of 16 or 20 sensors are fully hidden, so visible entries always remain. The guard does not change this protocol’s loss.

Primary intervals in Table I are unadjusted. As a post-review multiplicity sensitivity check, we also report 98.75% marginal percentile intervals for a four-comparison Bonferroni family, using 200,000 crossed seed/fold draws. A second random-number seed checks numerical stability. This adjustment does not remedy dependent training folds or missing acquisition-day labels (Supplementary Table S9).

Transfer reverses in identifier fold 4: NH3 MAE increases from 16.22 to 18.83 ppm and H2 from 25.70 to 26.36 ppm. Aggregate gains therefore do not imply benefits in every partition. The available records do not support attributing this reversal to a particular day or environmental condition.
Table IIa. Label-Budget Comparison, Farthest-Point Fixed Split; MAE (ppm), Mean ± SD

Table IIa expresses label efficiency in labeled two-gas concentration pairs, including fitting and validation. At 10 pairs, transfer approximately matches scratch at 20 for NH3 and ethylene and has lower mean CO error, but higher H2 error. These descriptive comparisons are not equivalence tests or a universal 50% label-saving guarantee. Pairs, exposure records and overlapping windows are distinct units.

At five pairs, NH3 shows essentially no mean benefit (86.39 ± 36.11 to 86.02 ± 34.16 ppm). An error near 86 ppm is 17.2% of its 0–500 ppm range and does not demonstrate useful precise quantitative calibration. Sparse calibration coverage and training variability are possible contributors, not established causes. This is consistent with NH3’s weak primary and component-ablation evidence.

CO ablations are variable: removing attention gives 10.27 ± 12.18 ppm and removing temporal masking 7.93 ± 14.86 ppm. Exploratory paired-seed 95% bootstrap intervals are [2.68, 16.94] and [−0.33, 17.00] ppm, respectively (Supplementary Table S10). Temporal masking is compatible with no effect; attention has a positive conditional mean contrast, but its large variability limits a robust component-benefit claim. Neither SD overlap nor these unadjusted intervals establishes a general physical mechanism.
Full-cycle

Representative seed-42 pretraining reruns on one NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 took 38.8 s for NH3/H2 (1,260 windows) and 19.9 s for CO/ethylene (735 windows), each for 60 epochs with batch size 64. Timings include model initialization and optimization but exclude data loading, scaling and checkpoint writes. They are per-model measurements, not reconstructed total campaign costs; checkpoints are reused across adaptation budgets. Software and timing details are supplied in the supplement.
Data and Code Availability

The NH3/H2 dataset is identified by Harvard Dataverse DOI 10.7910/DVN/LWUSKO [29]; the public CO/ethylene and drift datasets are cited in [15] and [16]. Study code is linked at https://github.com/ngdvan/Transfer-learning-Enose. The accompanying revision package contains the analysis scripts, split-audit records, unrounded result exports and representative compute measurements used here. Exposure-to-day mixture logs and environmental measurements were not recorded and are not available.

old: The authors program a sequence of single-gas and binary NH3/H2 conditions spanning 0-500 ppm for each gas. Nonzero concentration settings are 25, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 ppm. For each condition, the authors expose the array to the prepared gas mixture for 180 s, then apply a 700-s recovery period, giving an 880-s measurement cycle. The authors record the multichannel responses throughout exposure and recovery, using a nominal 2.0-s sampling setting in the acquisition interface. The response increases during gas delivery and returns toward its baseline during recovery. The authors repeat the acquisition protocol on six separate measurement days. The computer interface controls the programmed sequence and records the response channels for subsequent concentration-regression analysis.
new: We programmed single-gas and binary NH3/H2 conditions spanning 0–500 ppm for each gas, with nonzero settings of 25, 50, 100, 200, 300, 400 and 500 ppm. Each sequence starts at gas delivery and records the complete 180-s exposure plus 700-s recovery cycle (880 s total). The acquisition interface was configured for a 2.0-s sampling interval. Acquisition took place over six days, but the six Combination-ID partitions were not intended as day splits. Day-by-day mixture details were not logged, preventing a reliable exposure-to-day mapping and leave-one-day-out evaluation. Temperature and relative humidity were neither controlled nor measured. These facts are clarified by the acquisition team; no timestamp-based cadence validation or retrospective environmental measurements are claimed.
